evidence: Plaut. Men. 1085: sed uter vostrōrum est advectus mēcum nāvī? — Nōn ego. — At ego.
terms.comment: Latin answers with the pronoun and the negative alone, as English does with “not me”; the verb can be added: Nōn ego fēcī.

terms.gloss: start it: be the first to provoke
evidence: Ter. Ph. 13: vetus sī poēta nōn lacessīsset prior
Cic. Phil. 2.1: ultrō mē maledictīs lacessīstī
terms.comment: For “he started it”: lacessere is to provoke, to pick a quarrel; prior says who began, and ultrō that he began unprovoked. See also “provoke”.

phrases.latin: Nōn ambōs volō, sed uter vostrōrum est advectus mēcum nāvī. — Nōn ego. — At ego.
phrases.english: I don’t want you both, only the one of you who came with me on the ship. — Not me. — It was me.

phrases.latin: vetus sī poēta nōn lacessīsset prior
phrases.english: if the old poet had not started it

phrases.latin: Tū nē verbō quidem violātus … ultrō mē maledictīs lacessīstī.
phrases.english: Without being wronged by so much as a word … you started it, attacking me with abuse.

phrases.latin: Quis hoc fēcit? — Nōn ego, tata: ille mē prior lacessīvit.
phrases.english: Who did this? — Not me, Dad: he started it.

sources: Lewis & Short: ego · Lewis & Short: lacesso · Lewis & Short: prior · Lewis & Short: ultro
